_note: Market day at Valehold. Drafts 4.9.1 and 4.9.4, moved across verbatim. The afternoon linking passage and the rumours are in rumors.json.

arrival.act1:
Valehold is smaller than you had it in your head.

The main street runs from the north gate down to the river and takes under twenty minutes to walk. Flagstones, stone houses of two and three storeys along both sides, the ground floors almost all shops, flowers still out on the sills above. The market is held on the square by the river and spills off the square into the two lanes beside it.

The goods in early October still carry the tail end of summer. The last of the plums, the last picking of beans, heaped high in shallow wooden baskets. Beside them what has only just come in: walnuts, squash, apples by the basket, and the first of the pickling jars.

Three smells at once in the air. The damp off the river, livestock, and bread baking somewhere you cannot place.

Nobody knows you. Someone looks up as you go past because your face is new, and that is all it comes to.
arrival.act2:
The market is fuller today than it was last time.

The harvest is at its height and everything is stacked higher than it stood a week ago. There is a queue at the grain merchant’s stall and four carts standing by the timber yard. You hear two men arguing over a price, loudly, and both of them are laughing.

Apples have gone from “just in” to “everywhere”. A stallholder sees you pass, takes one and puts it in your hand, with no thought of being paid.

This time somebody knows you. After you have gone by, a head turns and says something to the person beside it.
arrival.act3:
There is less on the square, and no fewer stalls.

What sold fresh goods has gone over to preserves and stores: rows of jars, smoked meat, roots in sacks, firewood in bundles. A whole quarter of it is selling what the Feast of the Sacred Flame wants — new hearth tongs, kindling in sheaves, red cord for the children.

The air is much colder. Your breath hangs in front of you a moment before it goes.

act3Known: You pass the grain merchant’s stall and he nods to you. He knows you have come today to sell.
act3Unknown: You pass the grain merchant’s stall. He looks at your cart, then at you, then goes back to the customer he has in hand. He has not seen you this month.
arrivalTail:
The grain merchant’s stall is on the east side of the square and the timber yard is down by the river. Everything you brought today is on the cart.

Gregor did not come in with you. He drove the cart as far as the square and went back. He does not care for towns.
sellGrain:
The grain merchant pours out a handful of your wheat, rubs it open in his palm and puts his face close to it.

“The quality is fair this year,” he says. “Some of the holdings on the north slope had theirs sprout. Yours did not.”

He names a price. You can nod, or you can stand there and say nothing. Standing there saying nothing is how haggling is done here; he will name another price himself.

The scales are his. He settles on the spot once it is weighed, copper and silver in two separate cloth bags, counted out plainly.

The cart is lighter. You fold the empty sacks and put them back under the boards.
sellTimber:
The timber yard is by the river, against the wharf. Wood going out of the valley is loaded onto boats here.

The buyer walks once round your cart and knocks twice on a cut face with the back of his hand, listening to it.

“North slope oak,” he says. “Dried well.”
sellTimberMillridge:
“Millridge said you would be coming.” He adds: “I will make it four for you.”

You do not know when Henk spoke to him.
sellTimberPlain: He names the market price and not a coin over.
sellTimberTail: Unloading takes a while. The logs go off the boards one at a time and land in the yard with a dull sound.
nothing:
You walk once round the square.

You sell nothing and you buy nothing. You look at what grain is fetching, and what timber is fetching, and hear a few things said, and then you come back.

What was on the cart is still on the cart.

The trip cost you half a day, and you know the prices now. Next time you will know when to sell.
returnOpen: The road back is the road in, and the light has begun to go.
returnSold: The cart is a great deal lighter. The purse rides in an inside pocket and speaks once at every rut.
returnUnsold: The cart weighs what it weighed coming in.
returnTail:
You go through the day’s accounts once on the road. The numbers come out right, and you are thinking about something else at the same time: of the things said today, there are a few you had better not forget.

As you come in at the estate gate Gregor comes out from the stable to take the cart. He does not ask what you sold. He looks at the horses first.
